nameStory: Lentil vetch gets its name from its tiny seeds, which look remarkably like miniature lentils you'd find in your pantry. The word 'vetch' comes from the Latin 'vicia,' meaning 'to bind' or 'to twist,' referring to how these climbing plants wrap their tendrils around other plants for support. It's also called 'sparrow vetch' because small birds love to feast on those lentil-like seeds.
description: Lentil vetch is a delicate, climbing annual plant that scrambles up through grasses and other vegetation using tiny curling tendrils. This slender member of the bean family rarely grows more than 2 feet tall, preferring to weave horizontally through its plant neighbors rather than stand upright. Its small purple-pink flowers are followed by narrow pods containing 2-4 seeds that look just like tiny lentils. The whole plant has a soft, smooth texture that distinguishes it from its hairier vetch relatives.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 3-5 pairs of narrow, oval leaflets that feel smooth and soft to the touch, ending in branched tendrils that curl like tiny corkscrews

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale purple or pink pea-shaped flowers, usually just 1-2 per stem, about the size of your pinky nail and barely noticeable unless you look closely

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, smooth, narrow pods about half an inch long containing exactly 2-4 round seeds that look like miniature brown lentils

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Weak-stemmed climbing plant that uses curly tendrils to scramble through grass and low vegetation, rarely standing upright on its own

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Entire plant feels remarkably smooth and soft, lacking the hairiness found on many other vetches - run your fingers along the stem and leaves

habitat: Look for lentil vetch in disturbed areas like field edges, roadsides, waste ground, and cultivated areas throughout New England. It thrives in sandy or loamy soils and often grows mixed in with grasses and other weedy plants. You'll frequently find it scrambling through meadows, abandoned lots, and along the margins of agricultural areas.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin climbing through surrounding vegetation, with the first smooth compound leaves appearing.
seasonality.summer: Tiny pale purple flowers bloom from June through August, followed quickly by the development of small seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Pods ripen and split open to release the lentil-like seeds, while the annual plant begins to die back and turn brown.
seasonality.winter: The annual plant is completely dead, but seeds remain dormant in the soil until spring germination.

funFact: Despite being called lentil vetch, this plant's seeds are actually edible and were historically used as food during times of scarcity - they really can be cooked and eaten like tiny wild lentils, though they're much smaller and more work to collect than store-bought lentils!
confusionNotes: Lentil vetch is most easily confused with hairy tare, but a simple touch test tells them apart immediately - lentil vetch feels completely smooth while hairy tare is noticeably fuzzy. Memory trick: 'Smooth lentil, hairy tare' - if it's smooth, think lentil seeds; if it's hairy, think getting a hair in your food (tare sounds like 'terrible').
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name includes 'tetrasperma' meaning 'four seeds,' though the pods actually contain 2-4 seeds, not always four. This species is also known as 'smooth tare,' where 'tare' is an old agricultural term for weedy plants that grow among crops - farmers would separate the valuable grain from the unwanted 'tares.'
compareHints: Among New England vetches, lentil vetch is the smallest and most delicate, with the tiniest flowers and smoothest texture. While tufted vetch and hairy vetch have showy clusters of purple flowers, lentil vetch has just 1-2 inconspicuous blooms per stem. Common vetch is much larger and more robust, and hairy tare feels distinctly fuzzy compared to lentil vetch's smooth surfaces.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tufted vetch stands out from its vetch relatives by having the most densely packed, one-sided flower clusters that hang downward like purple bunches of grapes.

Among the vetches in New England, hairy vetch stands out for its distinctly fuzzy stems - tufted vetch has smooth stems, common vetch has larger individual flowers, and the smaller vetches like hairy tare have much tinier flowers and leaflets.
Common vetch stands out from its relatives by having flowers that appear singly or in pairs rather than in clusters like tufted vetch or hairy vetch.

Among New England's vetches, bush vetch stands out for its short flower clusters of just 2-6 blooms, while tufted vetch has long, showy spikes of many flowers and hairy vetch has dense, cone-shaped clusters.
Hairy tare stands out from its vetch relatives primarily by size - everything about it is smaller and more delicate.
Among the vetch family in New England, large yellow vetch is unmistakable due to its bright yellow flowers - all other local vetches have purple, pink, or white blooms.
Among New England's vetches, spring vetch stands out for its diminutive size - both the flowers and overall plant are much smaller than tufted vetch or hairy vetch.
Unlike other vetches in New England, fava beans are much larger, bushier plants that don't climb or sprawl.
